::: {#sol-three-optimizers}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
optimizers = {
    "SGD": lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.1),
    "momentum": lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.01, momentum=0.9),
    "Adam": lambda p: torch.optim.Adam(p, lr=0.01),
}
final_loss, test_acc = {}, {}
for name, make_optimizer in optimizers.items():
    mlp = make_mlp()
    final_loss[name] = train(mlp, make_optimizer(mlp.parameters()), 5, 32)[-1]
    with torch.no_grad():
        test_acc[name] = (mlp(x_test).argmax(dim=1) == y_test).float().mean().item()
print(final_loss)
print(test_acc)
```

[Adam](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/gradient-descent.html#def-adam),
with training loss `r sprintf("%.2f", py$final_loss[["Adam"]])`,
against `r sprintf("%.2f", py$final_loss[["SGD"]])` for plain SGD
and `r sprintf("%.2f", py$final_loss[["momentum"]])` with momentum.
It also classifies the most images of the [test set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-test-set) correctly,
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * py$test_acc[["Adam"]])`%.
Momentum and plain SGD end close together,
as @sol-momentum-long-run predicts:
[learning rate](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/gradient-descent.html#def-learning-rate) 0.01 with $\beta = 0.9$ moves like learning rate 0.1 on a steady slope.
A comparison like this depends on the learning rates chosen for each method,
so a fair one tunes each method's learning rate separately.

:::
